analogy.p: Imagine your personal data is a book you have lent to a library. The library (data controller) may only use it for the reason you lent it, must keep it safe in a locked room, must not keep it longer than agreed, must correct any mistakes you point out, and must let you look at what it holds. If the book is lost or damaged the library must tell you and the head librarian (the ICO) can punish it. The **Data Protection Act** is the set of library rules. The analogy breaks down because data can be copied without the original ever disappearing, so a 'returned' book may still have been duplicated, which is why the law also requires deletion and security.
analogy.t: Your data is like a library book on loan

bullets: The **Data Protection Act 2018 (DPA 2018)** is UK law that controls how personal data is collected, stored, used and shared; it works alongside the **UK GDPR**.
You need to know the **purpose** of the Act: to protect individuals' personal data and privacy and to make organisations responsible for handling it properly.
You need to know the main rules (principles) and be able to give a **real-world example** of each one.
You need to know the **rights** of individuals, especially the right to see their data and the right to have wrong data corrected.
You need to link the Act to **security measures** (1.4) such as encryption, passwords and access levels, because these are how organisations obey the 'secure' principle.
Typical questions: state the purpose of the Act, describe two principles, explain what a company must do or should not do, or decide whether a scenario breaks the law.
core.p: This point sits in OCR J277 section 1.6.2 (legislation relevant to Computer Science) and asks you to know the purpose of the **Data Protection Act 2018** and to apply it to scenarios. You must be able to explain what the Act protects (**personal data** about living, identifiable people), who it applies to (organisations that hold data, called **data controllers**), the key rules those organisations must follow (the **data protection principles**), the rights it gives individuals (**data subjects**) and what happens when the rules are broken. It is examined on Paper 1 (Computer systems), usually as a short describe/explain question or inside a longer scenario discussion.

bullets: Replaces the **Data Protection Act 1998**; the 2018 Act is stricter and gives individuals stronger rights.
Aim: **protect people's privacy** and make sure personal data is used in a way that is fair and safe.
It covers **digital data and paper records** that are kept in an organised filing system, so a paper patient file is covered as well as a database.
It applies to **all organisations** in the UK that hold personal data: businesses, schools, hospitals, charities, councils and the government.
Why it matters to society: reduces **identity theft and fraud**, builds **trust** in online services, and stops organisations treating people's data as free property.
Link to ethical issues in 1.6.1: privacy, surveillance, and the balance between useful services and data collection.
core.p: Computers make it cheap and quick to collect, copy and sell huge amounts of information about people. Without rules, a company could keep your address, health details or browsing history forever, sell it without telling you, or lose it through poor security. Personal data can be used for identity theft, fraud, discrimination, stalking or manipulation, so the law gives people control over their own information. The DPA 2018 is the UK's modern data protection law and replaced the older Data Protection Act 1998. It brings the European-style GDPR rules into UK law, and after Brexit these continue as the UK GDPR, which is read together with the DPA 2018.

bullets: **Personal data** examples: name, home address, email address, phone number, date of birth, photographs, bank details, **IP address** and other online identifiers, medical records, exam results.
**Data subject** = the individual the data is about (you, as a pupil, customer or patient).
**Data controller** = the organisation deciding what data to collect and what to do with it; it carries the legal responsibility for following the Act.
**Processing** is almost anything you can do with data: collecting, recording, storing, organising, changing, sharing, deleting.
**ICO** = Information Commissioner's Office: the regulator; individuals can complain to it, organisations may have to report breaches to it, and it can investigate and issue **fines**.
The Act protects **living** individuals only; data about a company or a person who has died is not personal data under the Act.
core.h: Key terms: personal data, data subject, data controller and the ICO
core.p: Four terms appear again and again in this topic, and mark schemes expect them to be used accurately. **Personal data** is any information that relates to an identifiable living person, either on its own or when combined with other information. The **data subject** is the person the data is about. The **data controller** is the organisation (or person) that decides why and how the personal data is processed, for example a school, an online shop or the NHS. The **Information Commissioner's Office (ICO)** is the independent UK regulator that checks organisations obey the law, handles complaints and can fine organisations that break it.

bullets: Special category data includes **racial or ethnic origin**, **political opinions**, **religious or philosophical beliefs** and **trade union membership**.
It also includes **genetic data**, **biometric data** (fingerprints, facial recognition used to identify someone), **health data**, and data about **sex life or sexual orientation**.
Reason for extra protection: if leaked or misused it could cause **discrimination, embarrassment, loss of job or danger** to the person.
Organisations need a clear lawful reason and stronger **security** measures such as encryption and tight access levels for this data.
Exam tip: if a scenario involves **patients, fingerprints or religion**, say it is sensitive data so needs extra care.
Link to 1.4 security: strong **encryption** of stored medical data and **access rights** limiting who can open patient files.
core.p: Some personal data is more sensitive because misuse could lead to discrimination or serious harm. The law calls this **special category data** and demands extra care and a stronger reason before an organisation can use it. Hospitals, trade unions and employers handle it regularly, so you should be able to give examples and explain why more protection is sensible. Many exam scenarios involve medical or biometric information, such as a gym using fingerprint scanners or a clinic storing patient records, so spotting that the data is sensitive is a good way to gain a mark.

bullets: **Lawful, fair and transparent:** there must be a legal reason to use the data, it must not be used in ways that harm or mislead people, and people must be **told** what is happening (privacy notice).

**Purpose limitation:** data is collected for **specified, explicit and legitimate purposes** and must not be used for something incompatible, e.g. a shop cannot sell your email list to advertisers if you only gave it for receipts.
**Data minimisation:** data must be **adequate, relevant and limited** to what is necessary, e.g. a library does not need your religion to issue a book.
**Accuracy:** data must be accurate and, where necessary, **kept up to date**; inaccurate data must be corrected or deleted without delay.
**Storage limitation:** data must not be kept **longer than necessary**, so old records are deleted or anonymised.
**Integrity and confidentiality (security):** data must be processed **securely** with protection against unauthorised access, loss or damage, using suitable technical and organisational measures.
**Accountability:** the controller is responsible for complying and must be able to **demonstrate** this, for example with policies, records and staff training.
core.h: The data protection principles (the rules organisations must follow)
core.p: The Act sets out principles that every data controller must follow whenever it handles personal data. OCR expects you to know them in plain English and to use them to judge a scenario. The easiest way to learn them is to ask what an organisation is allowed to do at each stage of the data's life: when it collects the data, when it uses it, how long it keeps it and how it protects it. The six principles are fairly stated as: lawful, fair and transparent; limited to a specific purpose; adequate, relevant and limited; accurate; stored no longer than necessary; and secure. A seventh idea, accountability, means the controller must be able to prove it complies.

bullets: Unlocked filing cabinet or weak password on a patient database → **security** (integrity and confidentiality) principle broken.
Keeping customer records for 20 years 'just in case' → **storage limitation** broken (not kept longer than necessary).
Using pupils' phone numbers collected for emergencies to send a charity's adverts → **purpose limitation** broken.
Holding an out-of-date address so letters go to the wrong house → **accuracy** broken.
Asking a customer for health details to buy a book → **data minimisation** (adequate, relevant, limited) broken.
Collecting data via a hidden tracking cookie with no notice → **lawful, fair and transparent** broken.
Model sentence: 'This breaks the principle that data must be ___ because ___.'
core.p: Examination questions rarely ask you to recite the principles; they describe a situation and ask whether the law has been broken or what the organisation should do. Practise matching a behaviour to a principle. If a doctor's surgery leaves patient files in an unlocked room, that breaks the security principle. If a gym keeps the details of members who left ten years ago, that breaks storage limitation. If an online shop asks for your date of birth to sell socks, it is collecting more than it needs, which breaks data minimisation. Always name the principle and then explain the link, because the mark is for the reasoning.

bullets: The lawful bases are **consent**, **contract**, **legal obligation**, **vital interests**, **public task** and **legitimate interests**.
**Contract:** an online shop needs your address to deliver the goods you bought.
**Legal obligation:** an employer must give pay details to HMRC.
**Vital interests:** sharing medical details to save someone's life in an emergency.
**Consent must be opt-in:** 'tick here to receive emails' is valid; a **pre-ticked box** is not.
Consent can be **withdrawn** at any time, for example unsubscribing from marketing emails.
For online services offered directly to children, the UK sets **13** as the age at which a child can give consent themselves; under that age a parent or guardian must agree.
core.p: An organisation cannot process personal data just because it wants to; it needs a lawful reason, called a **lawful basis**. The most familiar one is **consent**, where you agree to the use of your data. Under the modern rules, consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, and it must be given by a clear positive action such as ticking a box yourself. Pre-ticked boxes or silence do not count as consent, and people must be able to withdraw consent as easily as they gave it. Other lawful bases exist, so a company may use your data without your consent when it is genuinely needed.

bullets: **Right to be informed:** be told what data is collected, why, how long it is kept and who it is shared with.
**Right of access:** ask for a copy of your data (subject access request); normally answered within **one month**.
**Right to rectification:** have inaccurate or incomplete data corrected.
**Right to erasure** ('right to be forgotten'): have data deleted in certain situations, e.g. when it is no longer needed or consent is withdrawn.
**Right to restrict processing** and **right to object**, e.g. to direct marketing.
**Right to data portability:** receive your data in a common format and move it to another service.
Rights relating to **automated decision-making and profiling**, so a person can ask for a human to review decisions made only by software.
Rights are **not absolute**: some data may be kept for legal reasons or to prevent crime.
core.p: The Act gives individuals a set of rights over their own data so that they are not powerless. The most examined are the right to **see** what an organisation holds about you (a **subject access request**), the right to have mistakes **corrected** and, in some circumstances, the right to have data **erased**. An organisation normally has to respond to a request within one month, and it cannot usually charge for a normal request. These rights are the reason the accuracy and storage principles matter in practice: they give people a way to check and enforce them.

bullets: **Encryption:** scrambles stored and transmitted data so stolen files are unreadable without the key.
**Strong passwords, multi-factor authentication and access levels** so staff only see data they need for their job.
**Firewalls, anti-malware and software updates** to block attacks; **backups** so data is not lost.
**Physical security:** locked rooms, ID badges, shredding paper records.
**Staff training** and clear policies on handling data; **data retention** schedules to delete old data.
**Anonymisation or pseudonymisation** reduces risk, e.g. removing names from data used for statistics.
Some organisations must appoint a **Data Protection Officer** to oversee compliance.
core.h: Duties of organisations and keeping data secure
core.p: To obey the security principle, a data controller needs practical protection that matches how risky the data is. This is where the Act links directly to your work on cyber security. **Technical measures** use technology to stop unauthorised access, while **organisational measures** are rules and training for staff. Because a large share of breaches come from human error such as lost laptops or sending emails to the wrong person, training is as important as software. Organisations must also be able to show regulators what they did, which is part of accountability.

bullets: Report to the **ICO within 72 hours** of becoming aware of a breach that is likely to risk people's rights and freedoms.
Tell the **affected individuals without undue delay** when the risk to them is high.
The most serious fines can be up to **£17.5 million or 4% of annual worldwide turnover**, whichever is higher.
The ICO can also issue **warnings, reprimands and enforcement notices** ordering organisations to change their practices.
Individuals can **complain to the ICO** or seek **compensation** through the courts if they suffer damage.
Reputation damage and **loss of customer trust** can cost an organisation more than the fine.
Examples: a hacked company database, a laptop with unencrypted patient data left on a train.
core.h: Data breaches, the ICO and penalties
core.p: A **personal data breach** happens when personal data is lost, stolen, destroyed, altered or disclosed to the wrong people, whether by a hacker, a lost USB stick or a mistaken email. If a breach is likely to put people at risk, the controller must tell the ICO **within 72 hours** of becoming aware of it. If the risk to individuals is high, they must be told too so they can protect themselves, for example by changing passwords. The ICO can investigate, order improvements and impose large fines on organisations that fail to protect data, which acts as a deterrent.

bullets: Exemptions exist for **national security**, **crime prevention and detection** and **taxation**, as well as some **legal proceedings**.
Purely **personal or household use** (an address book on your own phone) is outside the Act.
**Journalism and research** have limited exemptions, balancing free expression and privacy.
Limits in practice: organisations in **other countries** may be harder to control, and many people never read **privacy notices**.
Regulators have limited resources, so not every breach is **detected or punished**.
Discussion point: the Act protects privacy but compliance adds **cost and effort** for small organisations.
core.h: Exemptions and limits of the Act
core.p: The Act does not mean that nobody may ever use personal data without permission. There are exemptions where the public interest outweighs individual privacy. Police and security services may process data for preventing and detecting crime and protecting national security, and some data used purely for personal or household purposes (such as your own phone contacts) is outside the Act. Recognising these limits helps you write balanced discussion answers about whether the law is effective or too restrictive.

bullets: Step 1: **identify** the data subject, the controller and the type of data (personal? sensitive?).
Step 2: **match** what happened to a principle or right using the exact wording ('kept no longer than necessary').
Step 3: **explain the consequence**: risk to the person, ICO action, fine, loss of trust.
Step 4: for 'what should they do' questions, give **specific measures** (encryption, delete old records, ask for consent).
Step 5: for discussion questions, give **advantages and disadvantages**, then a **justified conclusion**.
Use scenario words (school, pupils, patients) in every sentence so the answer is not generic.
core.h: Worked scenarios and how to think through them
core.p: A reliable way to approach scenario questions is to identify the three parties, the data and the rule. Who is the data subject? Who is the controller? What information is involved and is it sensitive? Which principle or right is relevant? Then write a short chain of reasoning: what the organisation did, which part of the Act it breaks or follows, and the consequence. This structure also works for 6-mark discussion questions, where you must give both sides, such as the benefits to customers of data protection and the costs and difficulties for the organisation.

bullets: **Computer Misuse Act 1990:** hackers who steal personal data commit a crime under that Act; the controller may also have broken the DPA if security was poor.
**Security (1.4):** malware, phishing, SQL injection and brute force can all cause data breaches.
**Networks (1.3):** encryption of data in transit with HTTPS; firewalls and access control.
**Ethical issues (1.6.1):** privacy, CCTV, location tracking, targeted adverts, big data and AI profiling.
**Storage (1.2):** cloud storage means data may be held in another country, which raises protection questions.
Quick law chooser: **personal data** → DPA; **hacking** → CMA; **copying software/music** → CDPA.
core.h: Links to other topics and the wider picture
core.p: The Data Protection Act connects to many other parts of the OCR course. It is one of three main laws in 1.6.2 alongside the Computer Misuse Act 1990 and the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988, and exam questions sometimes ask you to choose the correct law for a scenario. The Data Protection Act is about **handling data about people**, the Computer Misuse Act is about **unauthorised access to computers** and copyright is about **ownership of creative work**. It also links to ethical, cultural and environmental issues because of surveillance, cookies, social media tracking and the digital divide.

exam: Command words: **state** = short fact (1 mark); **describe** = say what the law requires with an example; **explain** = give a point plus a reason ('because'); **discuss** = both sides then a conclusion.
For a 'state the purpose of the Data Protection Act' 1-mark question write: **to protect personal data and privacy of individuals / to control how organisations use personal data**.
2-mark 'describe one principle' answers: name the principle (1) and add what it means or an example (1), e.g. 'Data must be accurate (1) and kept up to date (1)'.
3-4 mark scenario questions: each mark is a separate point linked to the scenario; use the names of the people and data in the question.
Always **link the breach to the principle** with the word 'because' (e.g. 'this breaks the security principle because the files were not encrypted').
6-mark extended responses are marked by **level of response**: Level 3 needs a balanced, well-linked discussion and a conclusion that is justified; avoid a list of unconnected facts.
Spot the party: **data subject** = person, **data controller** = organisation; examiners reward correct use of these terms.
Give **specific security measures** (encryption, access levels, strong passwords, locked cabinets, staff training) rather than 'make it secure'.
Do not mix up laws: personal data → **DPA 2018**, unauthorised access → **CMA 1990**, copying creative work → **CDPA 1988**.
Quote numbers only if sure: **one month** for subject access requests, **72 hours** for breach reporting to the ICO.
Check the mark count: 2 marks = two developed ideas; do not write an essay, and do not give one idea only.

mistakes.r: It controls HOW organisations collect, use, store and share personal data; they may use data lawfully, fairly and securely.
mistakes.w: The Data Protection Act stops anyone looking at your data.

mistakes.r: It protects personal data about identifiable living people only.
mistakes.w: It protects all data, including company secrets.

mistakes.r: Consent is one lawful basis; others include contract and legal obligation.
Hacking is the Computer Misuse Act 1990; the DPA is about how organisations handle personal data.
mistakes.w: The Act is about hackers and hacking.

mistakes.r: Data must be kept no longer than necessary and then deleted.
mistakes.w: Data can be kept forever in case it is needed.

mistakes.r: Name the measure: encrypt the data, use access levels and strong passwords, lock paper records.
Paper records in an organised filing system are covered too.
The data subject is the person the data is about; the organisation is the data controller.
mistakes.w: The organisation is the data subject.

mistakes.r: The ICO enforces the law: it investigates, advises and can fine.

summary: You must know that the Data Protection Act 2018 is UK law controlling how organisations collect, store, use and share personal data about living people, including its principles, the rights of data subjects and the penalties for breaking it. It matters because Paper 1 scenario questions ask you to judge whether an organisation has obeyed the Act and to suggest protective measures.

terms.d: Any information relating to an identified or identifiable living individual, such as a name, address, email address, photograph or online identifier.
The identified or identifiable living person that the personal data is about.
The organisation or person that decides the purposes and means of processing personal data and is legally responsible for complying with the Act.
Any operation performed on personal data, including collecting, recording, storing, using, sharing and deleting it.
The independent UK regulator that enforces data protection law, investigates complaints and can issue fines.
More sensitive personal data, such as health, biometric, genetic, ethnic origin, religion or sexual orientation data, which needs extra protection.
A freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous agreement by the data subject, shown by a clear positive action.
A legal reason that allows an organisation to process personal data, for example consent, contract or legal obligation.
A request by an individual to see the personal data an organisation holds about them; normally answered within one month.
The principle that personal data must be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary.
The principle that personal data must not be kept for longer than is necessary for its purpose.
The principle that data is collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not used in an incompatible way.
A security incident that leads to personal data being lost, destroyed, altered or disclosed or accessed without authority.
A statement that tells people what data is collected, why, how long it is kept and who it is shared with.
Scrambling data so that only someone with the correct key can read it; a technical measure to keep data secure.
The duty of the controller to take responsibility for compliance and be able to demonstrate it.

worked.ans: Not secure: laptop not encrypted so stolen data can be read, breaking the principle that data must be kept secure (2). Kept too long: 25 years of records breaks the principle that data must not be kept longer than necessary (2). Full marks need both a principle and a reason.
worked.q: A dental surgery stores patient records on a laptop which is stolen from a car. The laptop was not encrypted and the records had been kept for 25 years. Explain two ways the surgery has not followed the Data Protection Act 2018. [4 marks]
steps: Identify the data: patient records include health data, which is special category data, so extra care was needed.
Problem 1: the laptop was not encrypted. This breaks the principle that data must be processed securely (1) because a thief can read the data, so patients' privacy is at risk (1).

Problem 2: records were kept for 25 years. This breaks the storage limitation principle (1) because data must not be kept longer than necessary, and old records should have been deleted or anonymised (1).
Optional extra: the surgery must report the breach to the ICO within 72 hours.

worked.ans: They can ask to see the data held about them (1), have wrong data corrected (1) and in some cases have it deleted (1).
worked.q: Describe the rights an individual has under the Data Protection Act 2018. [3 marks]
steps: Choose three distinct rights and describe each in one line.
Right of access: can ask to see the personal data an organisation holds about them (1).
Right to rectification: can have inaccurate data corrected (1).
Right to erasure: can ask for data to be deleted in some situations, such as when consent is withdrawn (1).

worked.ans: Model answer (Level 3): The company must only collect data it needs and tell customers why, which takes extra effort and cost for encryption, training and handling requests. If there is a breach it must tell the ICO within 72 hours and may be fined up to £17.5 million. Customers benefit because they can see and correct their data, and secure storage reduces the risk of identity theft. Overall, the Act benefits customers greatly and also protects the company's reputation, so the costs are justified.
worked.q: A company wants to collect customers' details online. Discuss how the Data Protection Act 2018 affects the company and its customers. [6 marks]
steps: Plan: effects on company, effects on customers, then a judgement.
Company: must collect only data it needs, tell customers why (privacy notice), get valid consent where needed, keep data accurate and secure and delete it when not needed.
Company: costs of encryption, staff training and handling access requests; breach must be reported to the ICO in 72 hours; fines up to £17.5 million or 4% of turnover.
Customers: more control: can see, correct and ask for deletion of data, so they can trust the firm.
Customers: lower risk of identity theft because data must be secure.
Conclusion: benefits outweigh costs because trust and protection matter more than the extra work.
